items.title: Four doors
items.prose: Four doors, one car. You pick door 1. The host, who knows where the car is, opens two of the other doors, both goats. You switch to the one door left closed.
items.question: What is the chance you win? Give a fraction or a decimal.

feedback.correct: Switching wins whenever door 1 was wrong.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how often door 1 hides the car.

byKey.half: You split the chance between the two closed doors. The host avoided the other closed door on purpose.
byKey.stay: That is the chance staying wins.

explain.text: Door 1 hides the car with chance $\tfrac{1}{4}$, and the host can always open two goats. Otherwise the car is behind the one door he left shut. So switching wins with chance $\tfrac{3}{4}$.

items.title: A host with a habit
items.prose: The host knows where the car is. When the car is behind your door 1, he opens door 3 with chance $q$ and door 2 otherwise. When he has no choice, he opens the only goat door. You pick door 1 and he opens door 3.
items.question: Write the chance that switching to door 2 wins, in terms of $q$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $P(O_3 \mid C_1)$, $P(O_3 \mid C_2)$ and $P(O_3 \mid C_3)$, then use Bayes' rule.

byKey.fixed: You used the usual host, $q = \tfrac{1}{2}$. Keep $q$ general.
byKey.q-top: That is the chance door 1 hides the car. Switching wins when the car is behind door 2.

explain.text: $P(O_3 \mid C_1) = q$, $P(O_3 \mid C_2) = 1$ and $P(O_3 \mid C_3) = 0$, each car place having chance $\tfrac{1}{3}$. So $P(C_2 \mid O_3) = \dfrac{1/3}{q/3 + 1/3} = \dfrac{1}{1 + q}$. It runs from 1 when $q = 0$ to $\tfrac{1}{2}$ when $q = 1$, and switching never hurts.

items.title: Two draws from one box
items.prose: Four boxes hold three coins each: GGG, GGS, GSS and SSS. You pick a box at random and draw a coin: gold. You draw a second coin from the same box.
items.question: What is the chance the second coin is gold? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance the second coin is gold

feedback.correct: Weight each box by how often it gives a first gold.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. First find $P(\text{box} \mid \text{gold})$ for each box.

byKey.prior: You gave the boxes with gold equal weight, or used the chance of a gold first coin. GGG gives a first gold three times as often as GSS.

explain.text: A first gold has chance 1, $\tfrac{2}{3}$, $\tfrac{1}{3}$ and 0 from the four boxes. So the boxes now have chances $\tfrac{3}{6}$, $\tfrac{2}{6}$, $\tfrac{1}{6}$ and 0. The second coin is gold with chance 1, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and 0 from the first three: $\tfrac{3}{6} \cdot 1 + \tfrac{2}{6} \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} + 0 = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

items.title: A selective report
items.prose: A trader makes two trades, each a win with chance 0.55, independently. He reports only: “at least one of my trades won”.
items.question: What is the chance both won? Give a decimal to 3 places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the chance of two wins by the chance of at least one win.

byKey.first: That answers “my first trade won”. His report names no trade.
byKey.prior: That is the chance before the report. Loss-loss is ruled out.

explain.text: $P(\text{both}) = 0.55^2 = 0.3025$ and $P(\text{at least one}) = 1 - 0.45^2 = 0.7975$. So the chance is $\tfrac{0.3025}{0.7975} = \tfrac{121}{319} \approx 0.379$.

items.title: A left-handed boy
items.prose: Two children, each a boy or a girl with equal chance. Each child is left-handed with chance 0.1, whatever its sex, independently. You learn: at least one child is a left-handed boy.
items.question: What is the chance both are boys? Give a fraction or a decimal.

widget.label: Chance both are boys
widget.accept: Any form equal to $\tfrac{19}{39}$, or 0.487 to 3 places.

feedback.correct: The rare trait moves the answer most of the way to a half.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare how likely the news is from a two-boy family and from a mixed family.

byKey.third: You ignored the trait. A two-boy family has two chances to contain a left-handed boy.
byKey.half: You treated the left-handed boy as a named child. Both boys could be left-handed, so it falls a little short of a half.

explain.text: $P(\text{news} \mid \text{BB}) = 1 - 0.9^2 = 0.19$ and $P(\text{news} \mid \text{mixed}) = 0.1$. Prior odds of BB to mixed are $1 : 2$, so the posterior odds are $0.19 : 0.2$. The chance is $\tfrac{0.19}{0.39} = \tfrac{19}{39} \approx 0.487$.

items.title: Deriving the trait formula
items.prose: Generalise the last item: each child has a trait with chance $q$, whatever its sex, independently. You learn at least one child is a boy with the trait. Show that $P(\text{BB} \mid \text{news}) = \dfrac{2 - q}{4 - q}$.
items.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order.

lines.text: $P(\text{news} \mid \text{BB}) = 1 - (1 - q)^2 = 2q - q^2$, since either boy may have the trait
With $P(\text{news} \mid \text{mixed}) = q$, the likelihood ratio of BB to mixed is $\dfrac{2q - q^2}{q} = 2 - q$
Prior odds of BB to mixed are $1 : 2$, so the posterior odds are $(2 - q) : 2$

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with the chance a two-boy family fits the news.

byKey.lr: The ratio uses $P(\text{news} \mid \text{BB})$, so that line comes first.
byKey.odds: The posterior odds need the likelihood ratio first.
byKey.prob: Turning odds into a probability is the last step.

explain.text: With $q = 1$ every boy has the trait and the answer is $\tfrac{1}{3}$. With $q = \tfrac{1}{7}$, a Tuesday, it is $\tfrac{13}{27}$. As $q \to 0$ it tends to $\tfrac{1}{2}$.

items.title: Pricing against informed buyers
items.prose: A market maker sells a share to anyone who buys. It will be worth £101 or £99, equally likely. 20% of buyers know which and buy only if it will be £101. The other 80% buy with chance 0.5 either way.
items.question: Given that a buyer arrives, what is the share's expected value? This is the lowest ask that breaks even.

feedback.correct: A buy is evidence the share is heading to £101.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find $P(101 \mid \text{buy})$ first, then the expected value.

byKey.naive: You ignored the information in the buy. Informed buyers arrive only before a rise.
byKey.informed: You used the informed share as the whole update. Uninformed buyers dilute it.

explain.text: $P(\text{buy} \mid 101) = 0.2 + 0.8 \times 0.5 = 0.6$ and $P(\text{buy} \mid 99) = 0.4$, so $P(101 \mid \text{buy}) = 0.6$. The expected value is $0.6 \times 101 + 0.4 \times 99 = 100.2$. An ask below £100.20 loses money on average to adverse selection.

items.title: Three ways to hear about a Tuesday boy
items.prompt:
A parent has two children. Each child is a boy or a girl with equal chance. Each is born on one of seven equally likely weekdays, all independently. Find the chance both children are boys in each case, using likelihoods.

(a) You ask “Is at least one of them a boy born on a Tuesday?” and the answer is yes.

(b) The parent picks one child at random and tells you its sex and weekday: “a boy, Tuesday”.

(c) The parent, who has at least one son, picks one son at random and tells you his weekday: Tuesday.

Then explain in a few sentences why the three answers differ.
items.model:
Write BB for two boys and M for a mixed family (BG or GB). Before any news, $P(\text{BB}) = \tfrac{1}{4}$, $P(\text{M}) = \tfrac{1}{2}$ and $P(\text{GG}) = \tfrac{1}{4}$, so the prior odds of BB to M are $1 : 2$. Each child's weekday is independent of everything else, with chance $\tfrac{1}{7}$ for Tuesday.

**(a) You ask “Is at least one a boy born on a Tuesday?” and hear yes.**

- $P(\text{yes} \mid \text{BB}) = 1 - (\tfrac{6}{7})^2 = \tfrac{13}{49}$, since either boy may be the Tuesday boy.
- $P(\text{yes} \mid \text{M}) = \tfrac{1}{7} = \tfrac{7}{49}$, since only one child can be.
- $P(\text{yes} \mid \text{GG}) = 0$.
- Posterior odds: $1 : 2$ times $\tfrac{13}{7}$ gives $13 : 14$, so $P(\text{BB} \mid \text{yes}) = \tfrac{13}{27} \approx 0.481$.

**(b) The parent picks one child at random and reports its sex and weekday: “a boy, born on a Tuesday”.**

- $P(\text{report} \mid \text{BB}) = 1 \times \tfrac{1}{7} = \tfrac{1}{7}$: whichever child is picked is a boy.
- $P(\text{report} \mid \text{M}) = \tfrac{1}{2} \times \tfrac{1}{7} = \tfrac{1}{14}$: the boy must be the one picked.
- Likelihood ratio 2, so the odds become $1 : 2$ times $2 = 1 : 1$ and $P(\text{BB} \mid \text{report}) = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

**(c) A parent with at least one son picks one son at random and names his weekday: Tuesday.**

- $P(\text{Tuesday} \mid \text{BB}) = \tfrac{1}{7}$ and $P(\text{Tuesday} \mid \text{M}) = \tfrac{1}{7}$: the chosen son is equally likely to be born on any day.
- Likelihood ratio 1, so the odds stay at $1 : 2$ and $P(\text{BB} \mid \text{report}) = \tfrac{1}{3}$, the plain “at least one boy” answer.

**Why they differ.** The words heard are almost the same, but the procedure that produced them is not. In (a) a two-boy family passes the yes/no test through either boy, so it is favoured $13 : 7$. In (b) the report singles out one child, as “the elder is a boy” does, so the other child is a fair coin. In (c) a weekday would have been named in any case, so Tuesday carries no information about the sibling. The answer depends on $P(\text{what you heard} \mid \text{each family})$, and that is fixed by how the fact reached you.

rubric.text: Sets up the prior: BB, mixed, GG at $\tfrac{1}{4}$, $\tfrac{1}{2}$ and $\tfrac{1}{4}$, or prior odds BB to mixed of $1:2$.
In (b), finds the likelihoods $\tfrac{1}{7}$ and $\tfrac{1}{14}$ and reaches $\tfrac{1}{2}$.
In (c), sees that both likelihoods are $\tfrac{1}{7}$ and reaches $\tfrac{1}{3}$.
Explains that the procedure that produced the words sets the likelihoods, and so the answer.

items.title: Three hosts, any number of doors
items.prose:
A game show has $n \ge 3$ doors, numbered 0 to $n - 1$, and one car. The producers may not place the car evenly: `prior[k]` is the chance it is behind door `k`. You pick door `pick`. The host opens one other door, `opened`, and it shows a goat. Each host follows his own rule:

- `'knows'`: he knows where the car is. He opens one of the doors that are neither yours nor the car's, each with equal chance.
- `'random'`: he does not know. He opens one of the doors other than yours, each with equal chance. This time it showed a goat.
- `'lowest'`: he knows, and he always opens the lowest-numbered door that is neither yours nor the car's.
items.question: Write `host_likelihood(n, pick, car, opened, host)`: the chance that this host opens door `opened` and shows a goat, when the car is behind door `car`. Then write `door_posterior(prior, pick, opened, host)`. It returns the list of chances that the car is behind each door, given what you saw, or `None` if what you saw has chance 0.

widget.starter:
def host_likelihood(n, pick, car, opened, host):
    """Chance this host opens door `opened` and shows a
    goat, when the car is behind door `car` and you
    picked door `pick`."""
    ...


def door_posterior(prior, pick, opened, host):
    """Chance the car is behind each door, given that
    the host opened door `opened` and it showed a goat.
    None if that cannot happen."""
    ...


print(door_posterior([1/3, 1/3, 1/3], 0, 2, 'knows'))
widget.solution:
def host_likelihood(n, pick, car, opened, host):
    """Chance this host opens door `opened` and shows a
    goat, when the car is behind door `car` and you
    picked door `pick`."""
    if opened == pick or opened == car:
        return 0.0      # not your door; a car is no goat
    if host == 'knows':
        allowed = [d for d in range(n) if d != pick and d != car]
        return 1 / len(allowed)
    if host == 'random':
        return 1 / (n - 1)  # any door but yours
    if host == 'lowest':
        first = min(d for d in range(n) if d != pick and d != car)
        return 1.0 if opened == first else 0.0
    raise ValueError(host)


def door_posterior(prior, pick, opened, host):
    """Chance the car is behind each door, given that
    the host opened door `opened` and it showed a goat.
    None if that cannot happen."""
    n = len(prior)
    paths = [prior[c] * host_likelihood(n, pick, c, opened, host)
             for c in range(n)]
    total = sum(paths)  # chance of what you saw
    if total == 0:
        return None
    return [p / total for p in paths]


print(door_posterior([1/3, 1/3, 1/3], 0, 2, 'knows'))

tests.call: [host_likelihood(4, 1, c, d, 'lowest') for d in (0, 2) for c in range(4)]

widget.how: Check runs 11 hidden tests. Three check `host_likelihood` for each host on four or five doors. Eight check `door_posterior` on three to ten doors, with even and uneven priors. Each chance must match the exact value within a relative error of 1e-9.

feedback.correct: Each host's rule became one likelihood per car place, and Bayes' rule did the rest.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Work the first failing case by hand: one path per car place, prior times likelihood.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 is the classic game. With the car behind your door the host has two goat doors to choose from, so each has chance $\tfrac12$.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 has five doors. The knowing host has four doors to choose from when the car is behind yours, and three otherwise.
byKey.test-3: Test 3 is the host who does not know. He opens door 4 with chance $\tfrac14$ wherever the car is. But a goat showed there, so the car is not behind it.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 is the lowest-door host on four doors. If the car is behind door 0 he cannot open it, so he opens door 2 instead.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 uses an uneven prior. Weight each car place by its prior before you add the paths.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 is the random host with an uneven prior. Door 2 showed a goat, so its path drops out; the rest keep their prior shares.
byKey.test-9: Test 9 is the lowest-door host when you picked door 3. Opening door 1 means door 0 must hide the car.
byKey.test-10: Test 10 asks for `None` when what you saw has chance 0. When one path survives, its door gets chance 1.
byKey.test-11: Test 11 has ten doors and an even prior. Your door keeps $\tfrac{1}{10}$; the other eight closed doors share the rest.

explain.text: Each car place is one path on the tree: its prior, times the chance this host opens `opened` and shows a goat from there. Bayes' rule divides each path by their total, the chance of what you saw. The goat matters for the random host: his rule does not avoid the car, but the car cannot be behind a door that showed a goat.
